q: The mass spectrum of 2-butanone is shown. Which peak is the molecular ion?
h: Add up the nominal mass of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O. The molecular ion is not necessarily the tallest peak.
w: 2-Butanone is C4H8O: 4(12) + 8(1) + 16 = 72. The molecular ion (the radical cation of the intact molecule) is at m/z 72. The small peak at 73 is M+1 (about 4.4% of M, from 13C), and the base peak at 43 is the acylium ion CH3C≡O+.
x: m/z 43 is the base peak (most abundant ion), the CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> acylium ion from α-cleavage; the base peak is not the molecular ion.
m/z 73 is the M+1 peak, from molecules that contain one <sup>13</sup>C atom.
m/z 57 is M − 15, the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> ion formed by α-cleavage loss of a methyl radical.

q: An unknown aromatic compound shows a molecular ion at m/z 156 and a peak of almost equal height at m/z 158 (spectrum shown). Which element does this pattern indicate?
h: Which halogen has two isotopes, two mass units apart, in nearly equal amounts?
w: Bromine is about 50.7% 79Br and 49.3% 81Br, so a compound with one bromine shows M and M+2 peaks of nearly equal height. Here M = 156 fits bromobenzene, C6H579Br (72 + 5 + 79), and m/z 77 (C6H5+) is M − 79, loss of a Br atom.
x: One chlorine gives M : M+2 ≈ 3 : 1 (<sup>35</sup>Cl : <sup>37</sup>Cl), not 1 : 1.
Two chlorines give M, M+2 and M+4 in about 9 : 6 : 1; the M+2 peak would be smaller than M and an M+4 peak would appear.
Sulfur's <sup>34</sup>S is only about 4.4% abundant, giving a small M+2 peak, not one as tall as M.

q: Which compound gives the mass spectrum shown?
h: Find the highest-mass cluster and look at the height ratio of its two peaks.
w: The highest-mass peaks are m/z 78 and 80 in a 3 : 1 ratio, the signature of one chlorine (35Cl/37Cl). C3H735Cl = 36 + 7 + 35 = 78. The 63/65 pair (also 3 : 1) is M − CH3, which still contains Cl. The compound is 1-chloropropane.
x: 1-Bromopropane would show M at 122 and 124 in about a 1 : 1 ratio.
1-Chlorobutane would show its 3 : 1 molecular-ion pair at 92 and 94.
1,1-Dichloroethane (two Cl) would show M at 98, 100 and 102 in about 9 : 6 : 1.

q: Chlorine is about 75% <sup>35</sup>Cl and 25% <sup>37</sup>Cl. For a compound containing two chlorine atoms, what are the approximate relative intensities of the M, M+2 and M+4 peaks (ignore <sup>13</sup>C)?
h: Treat each Cl independently: P(35) = 3/4 and P(37) = 1/4. How many ways can you get one of each?
w: M (both 35Cl) = (3/4)2 = 9/16. M+2 (one of each) can arise two ways: 2(3/4)(1/4) = 6/16. M+4 (both 37Cl) = (1/4)2 = 1/16. The ratio is 9 : 6 : 1, a pattern seen for CH2Cl2 at m/z 84, 86 and 88.
x: 9 : 3 : 1 forgets that the mixed isotopologue can form two ways (<sup>35</sup>Cl/<sup>37</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl/<sup>35</sup>Cl).
1 : 2 : 1 is the pattern for two bromines, whose isotopes are nearly 1 : 1.
3 : 1 with no M+4 is the pattern for a single chlorine; a second Cl adds an M+4 peak.

q: A dihalomethane CH<sub>2</sub>XY gives the mass spectrum shown, with molecular-ion peaks at m/z 128, 130 and 132 in about a 3 : 4 : 1 ratio. Which halogens does it contain?
h: Combine Br (about 1 : 1) with Cl (about 3 : 1) and work out the probabilities for M, M+2 and M+4.
w: With one Br (½ : ½) and one Cl (¾ : ¼): M = (½)(¾) = 3/8; M+2 = (½)(¼) + (½)(¾) = 4/8; M+4 = (½)(¼) = 1/8, so one Br and one Cl gives 3 : 4 : 1. The mass fits too: CH279Br35Cl = 12 + 2 + 79 + 35 = 128. The fragments agree: 49/51 (3 : 1) is CH2Cl+ (loss of Br) and 93/95 (1 : 1) is CH2Br+ (loss of Cl).
x: Two bromines give a 1 : 2 : 1 pattern, and CH<sub>2</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> would appear at m/z 172, 174 and 176.
Two chlorines give 9 : 6 : 1, and CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> would appear at m/z 84, 86 and 88.
Fluorine has only one isotope (<sup>19</sup>F), so Br + F would give just M and M+2 at 1 : 1 (m/z 112 and 114), with no M+4.

q: An unknown containing only C, H, N and/or O shows M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 86 (relative intensity 15%) and an M+1 peak at m/z 87 (1.0%). Which molecular formula best fits? (Each carbon contributes about 1.1% to M+1.)
h: Number of carbons ≈ (M+1 intensity ÷ M intensity) ÷ 0.011.
w: (M+1)/M = 1.0/15 = 0.067, and 0.067/0.011 ≈ 6 carbons. All four formulas have nominal mass 86, but only C6H14 has six carbons. The fragments (57, 43, 71) fit a hexane, which loses alkyl radicals to give C4H9+, C3H7+ and C5H11+.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O has five carbons, so its M+1 would be about 5.5% of M (0.8% here), not 6.7%.
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has four carbons, giving an M+1 of only about 4.4% of M.
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>2</sub> has four carbons; even adding about 0.4% per <sup>15</sup>N, M+1 would be only about 5% of M.

q: An unknown that contains only C, H, N and O gives the mass spectrum shown, with M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 73. What does the odd molecular mass tell you?
c: It contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms
It contains an odd number of oxygen atoms
Its molecular ion is an even-electron cation
It contains an odd number of carbon atoms
h: Think about the nitrogen rule: which of C, H, N, O has an even mass but an odd valence?
w: The nitrogen rule: a molecule made of C, H, O, N (and halogens) has an odd nominal mass only if it contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms. Nitrogen has even mass (14) but odd valence (3), which forces an odd number of hydrogens. Here C4H11N (diethylamine) = 73, and its base peak at 58 is M − CH3 from α-cleavage next to nitrogen.
x: Oxygen has even mass (16) and even valence (2), so the number of oxygens never changes whether M is odd or even.
Every molecular ion formed by electron impact is a radical cation (odd-electron), whatever its mass.
Carbon has even mass (12) and even valence (4), so the number of carbons has no effect on whether M is odd.

q: α-Cleavage of the molecular ion (m/z 100) of 2-methyl-3-pentanone gives two different acylium ions. At what m/z values do they appear?
h: α-Cleavage breaks a bond between the carbonyl carbon and one of its neighbors; the positive charge stays on the C≡O<sup>+</sup> fragment.
w: Breaking the C(=O)–CH(CH3)2 bond expels an isopropyl radical (43) and leaves CH3CH2C≡O+, m/z 100 − 43 = 57. Breaking the C(=O)–CH2CH3 bond expels an ethyl radical (29) and leaves (CH3)2CHC≡O+, m/z 100 − 29 = 71. The acylium ions are at m/z 57 and 71.
x: 43 and 29 are the masses of the radicals lost (isopropyl and ethyl); when they appear as ions they are alkyl cations, not acylium ions.
58 and 72 would be McLafferty ions, which need a hydrogen on a γ carbon; neither alkyl group here has a γ carbon.
85 is M − CH<sub>3</sub>; loss of a methyl from the isopropyl group breaks a bond β to the carbonyl, so it is not α-cleavage, and the ion is not an acylium.

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O carbonyl compound gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> 100, base peak 43, and a strong peak at m/z 58. Which isomer is it?
h: An even-mass fragment from a C, H, O compound usually means a neutral molecule was lost. Which rearrangement does that, and what does it need?
w: The even-mass ion at 58 is a McLafferty fragment: a γ-hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen and the α–β bond breaks, expelling an alkene. For 2-hexanone, the butyl chain has γ-hydrogens; loss of propene (42) gives the enol radical cation CH2=C(OH)CH3+• at 100 − 42 = 58. The base peak 43 is CH3C≡O+ from α-cleavage (loss of ·C4H9), and 85 is loss of ·CH3.
x: 3-Hexanone undergoes McLafferty cleavage on the propyl side, losing ethene (28) to give m/z 72, not 58; its acylium ions are at 57 and 71.
3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanone has no γ-hydrogen (the quaternary α carbon carries only methyls), so it cannot undergo a McLafferty rearrangement; its base peak is the tert-butyl cation at 57.
Hexanal's McLafferty fragment is CH<sub>2</sub>=CHOH<sup>+•</sup> at m/z 44, after loss of 1-butene (56).

q: The mass spectrum of 1-pentanol shows a very weak M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 88 and a peak at m/z 70. Which process gives the m/z 70 ion?
h: Subtract: 88 − 70 = ? Which small neutral molecule has that mass?
w: 88 − 70 = 18, the mass of water. Alcohols commonly show an M − 18 peak from loss of H2O (dehydration of the molecular ion), and their M+ is often weak or missing. The peak at 31 is the α-cleavage ion CH2=OH+.
x: Loss of a hydroxyl radical (17) would give m/z 71, not 70.
α-Cleavage losing a butyl radical (57) gives CH<sub>2</sub>=OH<sup>+</sup> at m/z 31, not 70.
Loss of a methyl radical (15) would give m/z 73.

q: Which m/z value is expected for the base peak in the mass spectrum of 2-methyl-2-butanol (M = 88)?
h: Alcohols cleave at the C–C bond next to the C–OH carbon. When there is a choice, which radical leaves most easily?
w: α-Cleavage of an alcohol breaks a C–C bond on the carbinol carbon and gives a resonance-stabilized oxonium ion. Here the carbinol carbon carries two methyls and one ethyl. Loss of the larger ethyl radical (29) is favored and gives (CH3)2C=OH+ at 88 − 29 = 59, the base peak. Loss of ·CH3 gives a smaller peak at 73.
x: m/z 73 comes from α-cleavage loss of a methyl radical; it is observed, but loss of the larger ethyl radical is preferred.
m/z 70 is M − H<sub>2</sub>O; dehydration occurs, but for a tertiary alcohol the α-cleavage ion dominates.
m/z 71 would be loss of ·OH; C–O cleavage is minor compared with α-cleavage, which gives a much more stable oxonium ion.

q: An amine C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N shows a weak M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 73 and a base peak at m/z 58. Which structure fits best?
h: Amines undergo α-cleavage: a C–C bond on the carbon attached to N breaks, giving an iminium ion. 73 − 58 = 15. Which radical is lost?
w: The base peak at 58 means loss of a methyl radical (15) by α-cleavage. In tert-butylamine the carbon bearing N carries three methyls, so every α-cleavage loses ·CH3 and gives (CH3)2C=NH2+ at m/z 58.
x: 1-Butanamine loses a propyl radical by α-cleavage, giving CH<sub>2</sub>=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 30 as the base peak.
2-Butanamine preferentially loses the larger ethyl radical, giving CH<sub>3</sub>CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 44 as the base peak.
N-Methylpropylamine loses an ethyl radical from the propyl side, giving CH<sub>2</sub>=NHCH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at m/z 44.

q: The mass spectrum of 2,2-dimethylpropane (M = 72) is shown. The base peak is at m/z 57, and almost no molecular ion is seen. What is the best explanation?
c: The molecular ion easily loses ·CH<sub>3</sub> to give the tertiary (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> cation
The molecular ion loses a hydrogen atom to give the primary (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> cation
The molecular ion undergoes a McLafferty rearrangement and expels a neutral CH<sub>4</sub> molecule
The molecular ion loses ·CH<sub>3</sub> to give a primary carbocation stabilized by hyperconjugation
h: Alkanes fragment where the most stable cation can form. What cation is left when a methyl leaves the central carbon?
w: Alkane molecular ions cleave preferentially at branch points, because the resulting carbocation is more substituted. Breaking any C–CH3 bond in neopentane leaves the tertiary tert-butyl cation, m/z 72 − 15 = 57. This is so favorable that the molecular ion barely survives.
x: Loss of H would give m/z 71, not 57, and a primary cation is far less stable than a tertiary one.
McLafferty rearrangement needs a C=O (or similar π bond) and a γ-hydrogen; neopentane has neither, and 72 − 16 = 56, not 57.
The ion left after losing CH<sub>3</sub> is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>, whose charged carbon bears three alkyl groups: it is tertiary, not primary.

q: A mixture of 1-chlorobutane (bp 78 °C) and 1-bromobutane (bp 101 °C) is analyzed by GC-MS on a nonpolar column. Which describes the mass spectrum recorded for the first peak to elute?
c: Molecular-ion peaks at m/z 92 and 94 in about a 3 : 1 ratio
Molecular-ion peaks at m/z 136 and 138 in about a 1 : 1 ratio
Molecular-ion peaks at m/z 92 and 94 in about a 1 : 1 ratio
Peaks at m/z 92/94 and 136/138 together, because the MS records the whole mixture at once
h: The GC separates the components first; on a nonpolar column they come off roughly in order of boiling point. Then work out the M<sup>+</sup> pattern of that component.
w: In GC-MS the gas chromatograph separates the mixture, and the mass spectrometer records a separate spectrum for each component as it elutes. On a nonpolar column the lower-boiling 1-chlorobutane elutes first. C4H935Cl = 48 + 9 + 35 = 92, and one Cl gives M : M+2 ≈ 3 : 1, so the first spectrum shows m/z 92 and 94 in about 3 : 1.
x: 136/138 at 1 : 1 is 1-bromobutane, which boils higher and elutes second on a nonpolar column.
92/94 is the right mass for 1-chlorobutane, but one chlorine gives a 3 : 1 pattern; 1 : 1 is the bromine pattern.
The point of GC-MS is that the components reach the mass spectrometer at different times, so each chromatographic peak has its own spectrum.

q: A C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub> aromatic hydrocarbon gives the mass spectrum shown (M<sup>+</sup> 120, base peak 91). Which structure fits?
h: Alkylbenzenes break at the benzylic bond. 120 − 91 = 29: which radical is lost, and which isomer can lose it at the benzylic position?
w: Alkylbenzenes cleave at the bond β to the ring (the benzylic C–C bond), because the cation formed is a resonance-stabilized benzyl cation (which rearranges to the tropylium ion, C7H7+, m/z 91). A base peak at 91 means an ethyl radical (29) left from a benzylic CH2: propylbenzene.
x: Isopropylbenzene loses a methyl radical at the benzylic carbon, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sup>+</sup> at m/z 105 as the base peak.
4-Ethyltoluene loses a methyl radical from the benzylic CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, giving a methylbenzyl cation at m/z 105.
1,3,5-Trimethylbenzene has only methyl groups; its main fragment is M − CH<sub>3</sub> at m/z 105 (with M − H at 119), not 91.

q: For a compound that contains only C, H and O (so M is even), which statement about fragment ions from the molecular ion is correct?
c: Loss of a radical gives an odd-m/z ion; loss of a neutral molecule (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O) gives an even-m/z ion
Loss of a radical (e.g. α-cleavage) gives an even-m/z ion; loss of a neutral molecule gives an odd-m/z ion
All fragment ions have odd m/z, because every fragment ion carries a single positive charge
Fragment ions have even m/z only when the radical lost contains an oxygen atom
h: Every C, H, O radical has an odd mass (CH<sub>3</sub>· 15, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>· 29, ·OH 17). Every neutral C, H, O molecule has an even mass (H<sub>2</sub>O 18, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> 28).
w: An even-mass molecular ion that loses an odd-mass radical leaves an even-electron cation of odd m/z (e.g. 2-butanone 72 → CH3CO+ 43). Losing an even-mass neutral molecule leaves a radical cation of even m/z (e.g. 2-hexanone 100 → 58 by McLafferty; an alcohol M − 18). So radical loss gives odd m/z; neutral loss gives even m/z, a useful flag for spotting rearrangements.
x: This reverses the rule: subtracting an odd-mass radical from an even M gives an odd number.
Charge does not decide m/z parity; even-mass radical cations such as the McLafferty ion at m/z 58 are common.
Any radical made of C, H and O, with or without oxygen (·OH 17, ·OCH<sub>3</sub> 31), has an odd mass, so its loss still gives an odd-m/z ion.

q: A compound containing only C, H and O gives the IR and mass spectra shown (IR: strong band at 1717 cm<sup>−1</sup>, nothing above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> or at 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup>; MS: M<sup>+</sup> 86, base peak 43, other peaks at 58 and 71). Which structure fits?
h: The IR says what kind of carbonyl. In the MS, 43 and 71 come from α-cleavage, and the even-mass 58 needs a γ-hydrogen.
w: IR: 1717 cm−1 with no aldehyde C–H (2720 cm−1) and no O–H means a saturated ketone; M = 86 fits C5H10O. MS: 43 (CH3CO+) and 71 (M − CH3, C3H7CO+) are α-cleavage ions of a methyl ketone, and the even-mass 58 is a McLafferty ion (loss of ethene, 28), which requires a γ-hydrogen on a propyl chain. Only 2-pentanone fits all three.
x: 3-Pentanone has two ethyl groups: α-cleavage gives CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at 57 (its base peak), and with no γ-hydrogen it gives no McLafferty ion at 58.
Pentanal would show the aldehyde C–H band near 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>; its McLafferty ion appears at m/z 44.
3-Methyl-2-butanone gives 43 and 71 by α-cleavage, but its α carbon bears only methyl groups, so there is no γ-hydrogen and no McLafferty ion at 58.
